title: 408. Trigonometry & Periodic Models: Area of a Sector Using Radians
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Sector area from radius and angle
questions.learningObjective: Compute the area of a sector with the formula for an angle in radians.
questions.question: A sector has radius \(4\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(1.5\) radians. What is its area?
questions.explanation: For \(\theta\) in radians, the sector area is \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\). Here \(A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4^2\cdot 1.5=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 16\cdot 1.5=12\text{ cm}^2\). Omitting the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(24\text{ cm}^2\).

questions.concept: Sector area with an angle in terms of pi
questions.learningObjective: Compute a sector area when the angle is a multiple of pi.
questions.question: A sector has radius \(6\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) radians. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Using \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\): \(A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 36\cdot\frac{\pi}{3}=6\pi\text{ cm}^2\). As a check, the sector is one sixth of the circle, and \(\frac{1}{6}\cdot 36\pi=6\pi\). The value \(2\pi\) is \(r\theta\), the arc length in centimetres, not the area.
questions.hint: Square the radius before multiplying by half the angle.

questions.learningObjective: Find the central angle of a sector from its area and radius.
questions.question: A sector of a circle of radius \(5\text{ cm}\) has area \(25\text{ cm}^2\). What is its central angle, in radians?
questions.explanation: From \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\): \(25=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 25\cdot\theta\), so \(\theta=\frac{2\cdot 25}{25}=2\) radians. Forgetting the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) and solving \(25=25\theta\) gives \(1\), which is incorrect.
questions.hint: Substitute the known values into \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\) and solve for \(\theta\).

questions.learningObjective: Find the radius of a sector from its area and central angle.
questions.question: A sector has area \(18\pi\text{ cm}^2\) and central angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) radians. What is its radius?
questions.explanation: From \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\): \(18\pi=\frac{1}{2}r^2\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi r^2}{8}\). Hence \(r^2=144\) and \(r=12\text{ cm}\). Omitting the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(r^2=72\) and \(r=6\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\), which is incorrect.
questions.hint: Solve \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\) for \(r^2\) first, then take the positive square root.

questions.concept: Sector area with an angle in degrees
questions.learningObjective: Convert a central angle to radians before computing a sector area.
questions.question: A sector has radius \(10\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(72^\circ\). What is its area?
questions.explanation: Convert the angle: \(72^\circ=\frac{2\pi}{5}\) radians. Then \(A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10^2\cdot\frac{2\pi}{5}=20\pi\text{ cm}^2\approx 62.8\text{ cm}^2\). Substituting \(72\) directly gives \(3600\text{ cm}^2\), which is larger than the area \(100\pi\text{ cm}^2\) of the whole circle.
questions.hint: The formula \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\) needs \(\theta\) in radians; convert first.

questions.learningObjective: Find a sector area from its radius and arc length.
questions.question: A sector has radius \(8\text{ cm}\) and arc length \(5\text{ cm}\). What is its area?
questions.explanation: The central angle is \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}=\frac{5}{8}\) radians. Then \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 64\cdot\frac{5}{8}=20\text{ cm}^2\). Equivalently, \(A=\frac{1}{2}rs=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot 5\). The product \(rs=40\) lacks the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.hint: Find the central angle from \(s=r\theta\), or combine the two formulas into one involving \(r\) and \(s\).

questions.concept: Effect of the radius on sector area
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how sector area scales when the radius changes and the angle is fixed.
questions.question: The radius of a sector is doubled while its central angle stays the same. How does the area change?

options.label: B
options.text: It becomes four times as large.

questions.explanation: The original area is \(A_1=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\). The new area is \(A_2=\frac{1}{2}(2r)^2\theta=4\cdot\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta=4A_1\). Area depends on the square of the radius, so doubling the radius multiplies the area by \(4\); a factor of \(2\) applies to arc length.
questions.hint: Replace \(r\) by \(2r\) in the area formula and simplify.

questions.learningObjective: Find the area between two concentric arcs with the same central angle.
questions.question: A region is bounded by two concentric arcs of radii \(3\text{ cm}\) and \(5\text{ cm}\) and by two radial segments, with a central angle of \(1.2\) radians. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Subtract the smaller sector from the larger one: \(A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5^2\cdot 1.2-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3^2\cdot 1.2=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1.2\cdot(25-9)=9.6\text{ cm}^2\). Using \((5-3)^2=4\) in place of \(25-9=16\) gives \(2.4\text{ cm}^2\), which is incorrect.
questions.hint: Treat the region as a large sector with a small sector removed.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the sector area formula when the diameter is given.
questions.question: A circular pizza has diameter \(40\text{ cm}\). A slice is a sector with central angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) radians. What is the area of the slice?
questions.explanation: The radius is half the diameter: \(r=20\text{ cm}\). Then \(A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 20^2\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{400\pi}{8}=50\pi\text{ cm}^2\). Using \(40\text{ cm}\) as the radius gives \(200\pi\text{ cm}^2\), four times too large.
questions.hint: Find the radius from the diameter before using the area formula.

questions.learningObjective: Use the perimeter of a sector to find its angle and then its area.
questions.question: A sector has radius \(3\text{ cm}\) and perimeter \(12\text{ cm}\). What is its area?
questions.explanation: The perimeter is the arc plus two radii, so the arc length is \(12-2\cdot 3=6\text{ cm}\) and \(\theta=\frac{6}{3}=2\) radians. Then \(A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3^2\cdot 2=9\text{ cm}^2\). Subtracting only one radius gives an arc of \(9\text{ cm}\), \(\theta=3\), and the incorrect area \(13.5\text{ cm}^2\).
questions.hint: Remove both straight edges from the perimeter to find the arc length, then find \(\theta\).
